newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Heavy rains may cut Zimbabwe crop yields.
newsitem.headline: Heavy rains may cut Zimbabwe crop yields.

text.p: Continuing heavy rains in Zimbabwe may cut crop yields in the southern African nation's projected bumper harvest, industry officials said on Tuesday.
They told Reuters that many crops, including tobacco and the country's staple maize, were suffering from water-logging and soil leaching after six weeks of rains.

"We are going to have to revise downwards the figures that we have been expecting. Under these circumstances, we cannot continue talking about bumper harvests," said Nick Swanepoel, president of the main Commercial Farmers Union (CFU).
"Although we are still expecting good harvests, I don't think we should be looking at record-breaking figures," he said.
It was difficult at the moment to give any estimates, he said.
"But our national food security is not in danger because of last year's good harvests," Swanepoel said of 1996 when farming output rose by over 45 percent compared with the previous year.
Before the water-logging problems, Swanepoel and other industry officials were expecting Zimbabwe's maize output to surpass last year's record 2.6 million-tonne harvest.
"Some people are still hopeful...but I think that's being too optimistic," the CFU president said.
Weather experts are forecasting more rain this month, and Swanepoel believes it would damage the maize crop, cotton, groundnuts, sunflower and soyabeans.
Zimbabwe's flue-cured tobacco has also been hit by water-logging, and forecast production for the cropping season ending in April has been downgraded by up to 12 percent.

Agriculture Minister Denis Norman said last week continuous rains were causing soil leaching and water-logging in many parts of Zimbabwe, the world's third largest producer of flue-cured tobacco after the U.S. and Brazil.
The minister and industry officials had earlier in January forecast that Zimbabwe's tobacco output would increase to 240 million kg this season from 200 million kg last season.
On the positive side, the CFU president said the country's major dams were rising or full, ensuring adequate irrigation water for winter crops such as wheat.
